title: One blood, said in Athens
hookLine: Paul in Athens: all nations made of one blood, so contempt for a race denies the image of God
carry: one blood, every face God's image
last: A PREFERENTIAL LOVE FOR THE POOR.

lines: AN ALTAR TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.
cards: Paul is in Athens, and the city's thinkers have brought him up to the Areopagus to explain himself. He's been walking their streets, and he's found an altar with an inscription: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD."

So he starts there, with something of theirs. Then, partway through, he says a sentence that reaches far past that hill. God, he says, "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth."
Not Athenians and then everyone else. Not one people as the original and the others as copies. One blood.
Today, that sentence, and what it does to racism.

teach.h: EVERY FACE, THE IMAGE OF GOD.
teach.b: Paul's sentence stands on the first page of the Bible: "So God created man in his own image." Christians read that as true of every human face. Not some faces.
Then Acts adds the family tree: one blood, all nations. Put the two together.
If every person carries the image of God, and every nation shares one blood, then, in their reading, contempt for a race is contempt aimed at the image of God itself.
That's why Christians who oppose racism call it a sin and not only bad manners. It denies something God made.
Churches have not always lived this verse. Some Christians in history used the Bible to defend slavery and segregation.
Other Christians, reading the same Bible, worked and suffered to end both, and they quoted lines like this one as they did. The verse didn't change. What changed was who was willing to hear it.
Paul pushes it further in Galatians: "ye are all one in Christ Jesus."
And in the last book of the Bible, John sees a vision of a great multitude "of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues" standing before the throne.
Notice what's still there at the end. Nations. Tongues.
The differences aren't erased. Christians read this as oneness that isn't sameness: one family, every accent kept.

how: Christians teach this through the doctrine that every person bears the image of God; churches hold services and study groups on racial reconciliation, and some congregations deliberately bring together people of different races to worship side by side.

o: the blood of Christ shared at communion
an oath of loyalty sealed between two families
Paul's phrase: every nation shares one human family

p: every nation and tongue still there

s: Paul said "one blood" to a crowd in Jerusalem
he said it in Athens, at the Areopagus, after finding an altar to the unknown god.
the vision in the Bible's last book erases nations and languages
Revelation 7 shows a multitude "of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues": the differences are still there.
Christians in history read the same Bible on opposite sides of slavery
some used it to defend slavery and segregation; others quoted lines like Acts 17:26 as they worked to end both.

games.q: you're Paul, standing before the thinkers of Athens, who don't share your faith. where do you begin?
o: tell them their altars are worthless.
start with their own altar to the unknown god.
talk only about your own people's history.
games.why: he starts with their altar, and a few lines later he even quotes their own poets: "For we are also his offspring." one blood, spoken to people he started by honoring.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose race or family story is different from yours: a coworker, a neighbor, a classmate, a voice you listen to.

Ask yourself honestly what you've learned from them, and what you've never thought to ask; if a quick judgment about a whole group rises up, don't argue with it, just name it and set it down beside that one face.
If you pray, you can give thanks for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: One blood. Paul's words in Athens: every nation shares one family, and every face carries the image of God.

orig.note: Greek: blood; found in the Greek manuscripts behind the King James "of one blood" (Acts 17:26); many other manuscripts read simply "of one."
